title: Why Pineapple 'Eats You Back,' Why Fig Wasps Aren't Inside Your Fig Newton & Why Raw Kidney Beans Poisoned a Hospital — Bromelain (PDB 6YCF, 6YCG), Ficin & Parthenocarpic Figs (PDB 4YYQ), Noah (1980) & Rodhouse (1990) UK 80 °C Slow-Cooker Outbreaks & Red Kidney Bean PHA-L/E (PDB 1FAT, 3WCS)

teenKit.tldr: Plants are chemical warfare zones loaded with flesh-dissolving enzymes and toxins like bromelain, ficin, and lectins to stop animals from eating them. Cooking isn't just about flavor; it's a vital thermal defense that breaks down these destructive molecules before they attack your body.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding the hidden molecular warfare in your kitchen reveals that cooking is high-stakes applied chemistry keeping us safe from natural plant toxins every day.
keyTakeaways: Pineapples pack bromelain, a protease enzyme that digests meat and protein, which is why your tongue stings if you eat too much raw pineapple.

Fig wasps aren't crunching inside your Fig Newtons because most commercial figs are parthenocarpic (seedless without pollination), and traditional Smyrna figs use ficin enzymes to completely dissolve trapped wasps.
Undercooking red kidney beans in low-temperature slow cookers (around 80 °C) actually supercharges their PHA lectin toxins fivefold, causing severe poisoning instead of making them safe.

vocab.meaning: An enzyme that acts like molecular scissors, cutting up and breaking down proteins into smaller pieces.
A botanical term for fruits that develop and grow without needing to be pollinated by insects.
The process where heat changes the shape of a protein, destroying its biological function.
A toxic plant protein found in raw beans that causes cells to clump together and triggers violent gastrointestinal distress.

quiz.question: Why does eating a lot of fresh pineapple make your mouth feel raw and tingly?
options: Pineapple contains high amounts of citric acid that burn the top layer of skin off.
An enzyme called bromelain is actively breaking down the proteins in the lining of your mouth.
Tiny microscopic crystals in the pineapple fruit pierce the tongue tissue.
The high sugar content rapidly dehydrates the cells on your tongue.
quiz.explanation: Bromelain is a powerful protease that begins digesting the protein structures of your oral tissue the moment you take a bite.

quiz.question: What actually happens to the pollinating wasps trapped inside traditional Smyrna figs?
options: They crawl out through the bottom of the fruit before it is harvested.
They are frozen alive and preserved intact inside the dried fig skin.
They are completely dissolved and digested by the fig's ficin enzymes.
They hatch into larvae that consume the interior seeds.
quiz.explanation: Ficin is a potent protease produced by the fig tree that completely breaks down the wasp's organic matter into amino acids.

quiz.question: Why did cooking red kidney beans in a low-temperature slow cooker (around 80 °C) lead to a hospital poisoning outbreak?
options: The low heat allowed dangerous bacteria to multiply rapidly inside the bean broth.
Temperatures around 80 °C destroy beneficial vitamins while leaving toxins intact.
The slow cooker concentrated the bean's natural lectin toxins up to fivefold instead of destroying them like a full 100 °C boil would.
Slow cookers leach toxic heavy metals from their ceramic pots when exposed to legumes.
quiz.explanation: An 80 °C slow cooker fails to thermally denature the PHA lectin and instead supercharges its toxicity, requiring a full boiling temperature of 100 °C to neutralize it safely.
